item.content:encoded:
The World Baseball Classic may have only been a couple of weeks long, but its impact was felt all season long.
Pittsburgh Pirates ace Paul Skenes has not been himself this year. His velocity has dipped, his command has been off, and after posting ERAs of 1.97 and 1.96, respectively, over the last two seasons, he has a 3.91 ERA this season. Why? Skenes said part of it was the World Baseball Classic.
"There are a lot of other factors, so I don’t want to put everything on that," Skenes told the Post-Gazette. "But I feel like that was kind of the root of it a little bit."
This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.
The World Baseball Classic ran from March 3 to March 17 this year, and Skenes said at that time of year, pitchers aren’t throwing at max effort.
"Usually, that time of year, you’re kind of ramping up and it’s a little bit slow. You can kind of get onto the slope and find your body," Skenes said. "One live (batting practice), you’re topping at 97 (mph), and then the next you’re 98, 99. And that wasn’t the case this year. ... Looking back, I don’t think that really helped."
Early in the season, Skenes pitched well despite not having his usual 98-mph fastball. In 2024, his rookie season, he averaged 98.8 mph, and last season he averaged 98.1 mph. This year, he is down to 96.8 mph.
Skenes didn’t have a set number for how hard he wanted to throw; he just wanted to throw harder. The 2025 NL Cy Young Award winner said he made mechanical adjustments to try to improve his velocity, but nothing came of them.
"Unfortunately, it’s probably going to take an offseason to get it back," Skenes said. "Yeah, it’s just tough."
Skenes didn’t blame all of his struggles on the World Baseball Classic, but he believed it had an impact. He also said he isn’t the only pitcher who was impacted.
"It definitely affected the year," Skenes said. "Unfortunately, I don’t think I’m the only one."
The Pirates hope their ace will have a strong offseason, return to form in 2027 and help the team make a postseason push, assuming there is a season amid the impending lockout.

item.title: [Fox News] El as de los Pirates, Paul Skenes, achaca la caída de su velocidad al Clásico Mundial de Béisbol, en medio de una temporada complicada
item.dc:creator: Ryan
item.content:encoded:
{{#rendered}} {{/rendered}}
Puede que el Clásico Mundial de Béisbol solo durara un par de semanas, pero su impacto se notó durante toda la temporada.
Paul Skenes, el as de los Piratas de Pittsburgh, no ha estado a la altura este año. Su velocidad ha bajado, ha perdido precisión y, tras registrar unas medias de carreras limpias de 1,97 y 1,96, respectivamente, en las dos últimas temporadas, esta temporada tiene una media de 3,91. ¿Por qué? Skenes dijo que en parte se debía al Clásico Mundial de Béisbol.
«Hay un montón de factores más, así que no quiero achacárselo todo a eso», declaró Skenes al Post-Gazette. «Pero creo que, en cierto modo, esa fue un poco la raíz del asunto».
{{#rendered}} {{/rendered}}
El Clásico Mundial de Béisbol se celebró este año del 3 al 17 de marzo, y Skenes dijo que, en esa época del año, los lanzadores no lanzan a toda su capacidad.
«Normalmente, en esa época del año, estás entrando en forma y todo va un poco lento. Puedes salir a la pista y ir encontrando tu ritmo», dijo Skenes. «En una sesión de bateo con lanzamientos reales, llegas a los 97 (mph), y en la siguiente ya vas a 98, 99. Pero este año no fue así... Mirando atrás, no creo que eso ayudara mucho».
Al principio de la temporada, Skenes lanzó bien a pesar de no tener su habitual bola rápida de 98 mph. En 2024, su temporada de novato, alcanzó una media de 98,8 mph, y la temporada pasada, una media de 98,1 mph. Este año, ha bajado a 96,8 mph.
{{#rendered}} {{/rendered}}
Skenes no tenía una cifra concreta de a qué velocidad quería lanzar; simplemente quería lanzar más fuerte. El ganador del Premio Cy Young de la Liga Nacional de 2025 dijo que hizo algunos ajustes mecánicos para intentar mejorar su velocidad, pero no le sirvieron de nada.
«Por desgracia, probablemente me vaya a llevar toda la temporada baja recuperarme», dijo Skenes. «Sí, es duro».
{{#rendered}} {{/rendered}}
Skenes no achacó todas sus dificultades al Clásico Mundial de Béisbol, pero creía que había influido. También dijo que no es el único lanzador al que le ha afectado.
«Sin duda, eso ha afectado al año», dijo Skenes. «Por desgracia, no creo que sea el único».
{{#rendered}} {{/rendered}}
Los Pirates esperan que su as tenga una buena pretemporada, recupere su mejor nivel en 2027 y ayude al equipo a meterse en los playoffs, siempre y cuando haya temporada a pesar del cierre patronal que se avecina.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Paul Skenes gets called out for World Baseball Classic excuse
item.dc:creator: Matt Larter
item.description: MLB fans and analysts aren't buying Pittsburgh Pirates ace Paul Skenes' explanation for his rocky 2026 season, after the star pitcher pointed to his World Baseball Classic appearance as the root cause of his struggles. Skenes claimed that pitching for Team USA at the WBC sapped his velocity and set off his decline this season, calling it the "root" of his issues. item.content:encoded:
MLB fans and analysts aren't buying Pittsburgh Pirates ace Paul Skenes' explanation for his rocky 2026 season, after the star pitcher pointed to his World Baseball Classic appearance as the root cause of his struggles.
Skenes claimed that pitching for Team USA at the WBC sapped his velocity and set off his decline this season, calling it the "root" of his issues. But critics were quick to point out that his statistics tell a different story.
Skenes' excuse doesn't match the numbers
Mar 3, 2026; Scottsdale, AZ, USA; Team USA pitcher Paul Skenes against the San Francisco Giants during a spring training game at Scottsdale Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Mark J. Rebilas-Imagn Images
Through his first nine starts of 2026, Skenes posted a 1.98 ERA — nearly identical to his starts at the same point in 2025 (1.97 ERA) and 2024 (1.96 ERA). His performance didn't actually dip until mid-May, well after his WBC appearances were behind him.
Since that mid-May turning point, Skenes has posted an ERA of 4.73, a steep decline that has pushed his overall mark for the season to a career-worst 3.91, along with a 1.13 WHIP through 31 games. The reigning National League Cy Young Award winner appeared twice for Team USA at the WBC, striking out seven over four scoreless innings against Mexico in round robin play and throwing 4.1 innings in a 2-1 semifinal win over the Dominican Republic.
Pirates season winds down out of contention
Aug 9, 2026; Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, USA; Pittsburgh Pirates pitcher Paul Skenes (30) walks out to the bullpen before the game against the New York Mets at PNC Park. Mandatory Credit: Charles LeClaire-Imagn Images
Skenes' individual struggles have played out against the backdrop of a disappointing Pirates campaign. Pittsburgh sits at 79-77 with just six games remaining, firmly out of playoff contention. The team is third in the National League Central, a massive 19 games behind the division-leading Milwaukee Brewers (98-58), and seven games back of the Philadelphia Phillies (86-70) for the final NL Wild Card spot.
The Pirates begin the penultimate series of their season on Tuesday, hosting the St. Louis Cardinals as they look to close out a forgettable year on a better note.

item.content:encoded:
Pirates' Paul Skenes Explains How World Baseball Classic Held Him Back
Paul Skenes is still Paul Skenes, but the Pittsburgh Pirates superstar right-hander is having a down year by his standards.
What's the core reason for Skenes' 2026 performance? Well, the 2025 National League Cy Young Award winner thinks the 2026 World Baseball Classic "definitely affected the year" and "was kind of the root" of his struggles.
"Usually, that time of year [early March], you’re kind of ramping up and it’s a little bit slow. You can kind of get onto the slope and find your body. One live [batting practice], you’re topping at 97 [mph], and then the next you’re 98, 99. And that wasn’t the case this year. ... Looking back, I don’t think that really helped," Skenes said in an interview with the Pittsburgh Post-Gazette.
Skenes found success in the 2026 World Baseball Classic, which took place from early-to-mid March. Over two starts for Team USA, he recorded a 1.08 ERA, an 0.96 WHIP and nine strikeouts over 8 ⅓ innings pitched, holding opponents to a .226 batting average.
Among the talking points surrounding Skenes this season has been his slight dip in velocity. Granted, his four-seam fastball is still registering in the mid-to-high 90s on the radar gun.
"When you go outing to outing, you don’t really see the big picture sometimes. And I think looking back, I can kind of see it now," Skenes said. "Because early in the season, you can get away with stuff mechanically, or you might not be moving perfectly, but you’re fresh and the velocity is there because you’re feeling good. … You can’t get away with that in July and August and September."
Through 31 starts, Skenes has recorded a 3.91 ERA, a 1.13 WHIP and a 114 ERA+, while totaling 192 strikeouts and 3.1 wins above replacement over 168.0 innings pitched.
For context, Skenes posted an NL-best 1.97 ERA, 0.95 WHIP and 226 ERA+ last year, while totaling 216 strikeouts and eight wins above replacement. In 2025, Skenes gave up 11 home runs. This year, he has surrendered 19 home runs.
Paul Skenes has been an All-Star in each of his three seasons in the sport. (Photo by Daniel Shirey/WBCI/MLB Photos via Getty Images)
Moreover, Skenes posted a 1.96 ERA, an 0.95 WHIP and a 211 ERA+ over 23 starts in his 2024 rookie campaign (133.0 innings pitched), while racking up 170 strikeouts, 5.8 wins above replacement and finishing third in NL Cy Young Award voting.
"Stuff changes over the course of the season and from outing to outing. With that said, there’s been a lot more changes, outing to outing this year, that I kind of just don’t have an answer for body-wise," Skenes expressed.
Skenes and the Pirates are 79-77. While eliminated from playoff contention, Pittsburgh has the chance to post its first winning season since 2018.

item.content:encoded:
Los señalamientos sobre la temporalidad del Clásico Mundial de Béisbol han vuelto a crear controversia en la MLB, especialmente por los comentarios de Paul Skenes, el Novato del Año en 2024 y ganador del Premio Cy Young en 2025 dentro de la Liga Nacional, quien apuntó al torneo como responsable sobre su bajo desempeño, disminuyendo su velocidad y empeorando su efectividad.
¿Qué dijo Paul Skenes del Clásico Mundial?
“Hay un montón de factores, así que no quiero poner toda la responsabilidad en eso”, dijo Skenes el fin de semana al Post-Gazette de Pittsburgh. “Pero siento que esa fue, un poco, la raíz de todo el asunto”.
El Clásico Mundial ha sido constantemente señalado por su temporalidad respecto a la temporada de las Grandes Ligas. Celebrándose durante los entrenamientos primaverales de cada tres o cuatro años, los peloteros a veces acusan que el torneo les exige un máximo esfuerzo cuando apenas están terminando su preparación luego de cinco meses de receso invernal.
Paul Skenes on the World Baseball Classic and its impact on his velocity and effectiveness this season, via @colin_beazley:
"There are a lot of other factors, so I don’t want to put everything on that. But I feel like that was kind of the root of it a little bit."
"It… pic.twitter.com/wHZ002GU9O
Skenes apenas lanzó 8.1 entradas y solamente admitió una carrera para ayudar a Estados Unidos a llegar a la gran final. Paul ganó sus dos aperturas mostrando un gran control con 9 ponches y solo una base por bolas.
Al principio de la temporada, Skenes dijo que la disminución de su velocidad era intencional. Con el paso de sus aperturas, las semanas y los meses, Skenes tuvo que admitir que no sabía exactamente qué había pasado.
Ahora, Skenes tiene una respuesta contundente.
Rafael Devers takes Paul Skenes to deep center for a three-run shot! pic.twitter.com/FHLSnUmYlN
— Talkin' Baseball (@TalkinBaseball_) September 1, 2026
“Regularmente, en esa época del año, te estás preparando (para la temporada) y el proceso suele ser un poco lento. Puedes, en cierto modo, adentrarte en la pendiente y encontrar tu ritmo”, agregó Skenes. “En una práctica puedes estar rozando las 97 mph y la siguiente estás tirando 98 o 99 mph. Y ese no fue mi caso este año”.
Paul Skenes, venido a menos tras el Clásico Mundial
El vigente ganador del Premio Cy Young tiene una efectividad de 3.91 esta temporada, casi dos carreras más que el 1.97 de carreras admitidas que promedió durante la temporada anterior. Su velocidad ha bajado y su comando se ha perdido.
Su poderosa recta, que en 2024 tuvo un promedio de 98.8 mph, según Statcast, un año después bajó a 98.1 mph y esta temporada cayó significativamente hasta promediar 96.8 mph.
The @Cubs get to Skenes and take a 3-run lead! pic.twitter.com/LE1tWKNEqU
— FOX Sports: MLB (@MLBONFOX) July 26, 2026
“Cuando vas salida tras salida, a veces no ves el panorama completo. Y creo que, al mirar atrás, ahora sí puedo verlo”, dijo Skenes. “Porque al principio de la temporada puedes salir con algunos detalles en la mecánica o no moverte a la perfección; estás fresco y la velocidad está ahí porque te sientes bien. Pero eso no funciona en julio, agosto y septiembre”.
Un sector de la fanaticada comentó en redes sociales que los comentarios de Skenes parecen una campaña en contra del torneo, especialmente cuando existen casos de éxito de peloteros que participaron en el Clásico Mundial y están brillando en las Grandes Ligas.
El ejemplo más claro es el de Eduardo Rodríguez, que luego de ayudar a Venezuela a ganar el Clásico Mundial está teniendo el mejor año de su carrera al firmar una efectividad de 2.89 con los Diamondbacks antes de comenzar la última semana de la temporada regular; sus 15 juegos ganados es la mejor para él desde 2019.
Pese a la muestra, Skenes cree que no es el único afectado por el Clásico Mundial.
“Definitivamente afectó el año”, dijo Skenes. “Lamentablemente, no creo ser el único”.

item.content:encoded:
You know that the Pittsburgh Pirates’ offseason has officially arrived when we’re talking about a potential Paul Skenes trade.
It’s been a bit, hasn’t it? The Pirates remained in NL Wild Card contention throughout the second half, which ordinarily would be enough to halt the annual speculation. But Skenes has looked nothing like his Cy Young self, and he could realistically end the year with an ERA above 4.00. This is the same pitcher who had a 1.96 ERA through his first 320.2 innings and looked unhittable most nights.
In the grand scheme of things, nothing has changed. Skenes hasn’t publicly requested a trade, and the Pirates have insisted they won’t trade the three-time All-Star. Objectively, we imagine he’ll be toeing the mound on Opening Day 2027, whenever that might be.
Bleacher Report’s Zachary D. Rymer nonetheless pitched (pun intended) two possible Skenes trades, one involving the Yankees and another featuring Mets. Needless to say, we have plenty of thoughts.
Yankees send Ben Rice, Spencer Jones, and two pitchers to the Pirates for Paul Skenes and Bryan Reynolds
Pirates grade: C+
Yankees grade: C-
Those who spend much of their free time scrolling X/Twitter (hey, we know the feeling all too well) are likely familiar with the meme of Bugs Bunny squinting his eyes and saying “No.” That’s exactly how we felt upon initially seeing this trade offer.
Let’s start with the obvious: the Yankees aren’t trading Rice. At no point did we hear his name floated amid the Tarik Skubal rumors, and his left-handed power makes him a perfect fit for Yankee Stadium’s short porch. He’ll either open next season as the starting first baseman or designated hitter, depending on what Giancarlo Stanton’s future looks like; the 2017 NL MVP has one year left on his deal, and he’s been an injury liability since the start of 2019.
We’re skeptical that Jones would be moved unless the return involves an MVP-caliber outfielder. Trent Grisham is a pending free agent, and we’re genuinely unsure what Jasson Domínguez’s future in New York looks like, especially after his recent demotion to Triple-A. When a team doesn’t want you on the big-league roster ahead of the playoffs, what does that say?
Reynolds has had a fine year, and he entered Sunday leading the league in doubles. But if you’re the Yankees, do you really want to give up Jones and Lagrange for an outfielder who turns 32 in January? Reynolds is under contract through 2030 (with a $20 million team option for 2031), and that’s a significant commitment to someone who, at his best, is a mid-3 bWAR player.
We must also note that Rymer claimed that Rodríguez ranked No. 82 and Lagrange placed No. 100 on MLB Pipeline, which is simply untrue. Shortstop Dax Kilby is the only Yankees player on the most recent MLB Pipeline list, and he placed No. 83. So the Pirates wouldn’t even be landing a top-100 prospect? Hard pass.
That said, we’ll give the Yankees a C- for their return, because an elite Skenes ranks among the game’s best pitchers. But will we see him regain that 2024-25 form? That we’re even asking the question should say enough.
Mets give up Carson Benge and two prospects for Pirates teammates Paul Skenes and Bryan Reynolds
Pirates grade: D
Mets grade: C
At least the proposed Pirates-Yankees trade made some sense. We can’t say the same about Pittsburgh theoretically shipping Skenes and Reynolds to the Mets for Benge, Rojas, and Tong.
First off, why would the Mets only need to give up three players rather than the Yankees’ four? Rymer listed Rojas as the No. 79 prospect and Tong at No. 88, neither of which is accurate; Rojas is No. 73, and MLB Pipeline no longer lists Tong among its top 100 prospects, for reasons we don’t understand. Mariners lefty Kade Anderson has thrown 25.1 big-league innings, and he's still ranked No. 5, but Tong and his 39.2 innings over two seasons no longer qualify. Huh?
Benge has quietly enjoyed a solid rookie season, hitting .276 with 19 home runs, 61 RBIs, 22 steals, and a .760 OPS through his first 149 games. But for him to be the centerpiece of a deal involving both Skenes and Reynolds is absurd. Oh, and Benge turns 24 in January, so he’d be a slightly older second-year starter.
As for the Mets, adding yet another long-term contract isn’t the answer to putting their disastrous 2026 season behind them. As we’ve said before, Bo Bichette would be foolish to exercise his opt-out clause and leave $42 million in guaranteed money on the table. Marcus Semien has two years and $46 million left on his deal, and we’re not even factoring in Francisco Lindor’s contract.
That said, we’ve seen enough positives from Benge thus far to hold off on giving the Pirates’ theoretical return an “F” grade. But both teams should pass on even contemplating such an offer.

item.content:encoded:
Despite an active offseason and a busy trade deadline, the Pittsburgh Pirates were officially eliminated from postseason contention this past weekend. At 79-77, they have a chance to finish with a winning record for the first time since 2018, but that is the smallest of consolations. The Pirates made moves intending to contend this year, but missed the postseason.
One reason -- maybe the biggest reason, but not the only reason -- that the Pirates missed the postseason is a down year by reigning Cy Young winner Paul Skenes. A down year that included some outright bad stretches. Skenes has a 3.91 ERA in 168 innings this season, but from May 17 to July 31, he had a 14-start stretch with a 5.18 ERA. Pittsburgh went 3-11 in those 14 games.
Over the weekend, Skenes acknowledged that the World Baseball Classic may have contributed to his fluctuating velocity and down year because it interrupted his usual spring training buildup.
"There are a lot of other factors, so I don't want to put everything on that, but I feel like that was kind of the root of it a little bit," Skenes told the Pittsburgh Post-Gazette. "Usually that time of year, you're kind of ramping up and it's a little bit slow. You can kind of get onto the slope and find your body. One live (batting practice), you're topping at 97, and then the next you're 98, 99. And that wasn't the case this year. Looking back, I don't think that really helped."
Skenes made two starts for Team USA in the WBC, which has strict pitch limits and rest requirements, and allowed one run in 8 ⅓ innings. He did not make it out of the first inning on Opening Day, in part because his defense betrayed him, then Skenes put together a dominant eight-start stretch in which he pitched to a 1.09 ERA and averaged over six innings per start.
The rough stretch began after that, as did the velocity decline. And to be clear, Skenes still threw very hard. There were just more 95s and 96s and fewer 98s and 99s. Overall, Skenes averaged 96.8 mph with his fastball this year, down from 98.2 mph last year and 98.9 mph the year before that. He did not throw a single 100 mph pitch for the first time in his three MLB seasons.
"I didn't really have a number on it, but I would have liked to throw harder than I have this year," Skenes told the Post-Gazette. "Unfortunately, it's probably going to take an offseason to get (the velocity) back. Yeah, it's just tough."
The single most important thing is health and there's no chance -- zero -- the Pirates would have allowed Skenes to continue taking the ball every fifth day if there was a known injury. More than anything, his mechanics seemed out of whack, and mechanical fixes aren't always quick and easy, especially in-season. How much the WBC contributed to that, we don't know, but Skenes believes it was a factor.
Several other pitchers who participated in the WBC have had down years, including Skenes' USA teammate Logan Webb, but there's also a long list of pitchers who have thrived after the WBC. Nolan McLean, Eduardo Rodriguez, Cristopher Sánchez, and Yoshinobu Yamamoto are among them. They played in the WBC and have been among baseball's best pitchers in 2026.
Skenes, 24, is 14th among all pitchers in WAR despite his down season. He is looking at a record payday for a pitcher in his first year of arbitration eligibility this offseason. Skenes will become a free agent after the 2029 season.

item.content:encoded:
Paul Skenes Blames WBC Play for Affecting Velocity Drop in 2026 MLB Season
Paul Skenes' drop in velocity has been a major storyline surrounding the Pittsburgh Pirates this season, and he placed some of the blame on pitching in the World Baseball Classic.
"There are a lot of other factors, so I don't want to put everything on that," the Pittsburgh Pirates ace said, per Colin Beazley of the Pittsburgh Post-Gazette. "But I feel like that was kind of the root of it a little bit."
He said the drop in velocity was initially intentional, but he was never able to fully ramp up to his typical level.
"Usually, that time of year, you're kind of ramping up and it's a little bit slow," Skenes explained. "You can kind of get onto the slope and find your body. One live [batting practice], you're topping at 97 [mph], and then the next you're 98, 99. And that wasn't the case this year. ... Looking back, I don't think that really helped."
Skenes has still been solid this season with a 3.91 ERA, 1.13 WHIP and 192 strikeouts in 168 innings. In fact, the vast majority of the starting pitchers across the league would take those numbers.
But the vast majority of the pitchers across the league aren't Skenes.
The right-hander broke onto the major league scene in 2024 as the National League Rookie of the Year who finished third in Cy Young voting with a 1.96 ERA, 0.95 WHIP and 170 strikeouts in 133 innings.
He was even better in his second year as the NL Cy Young winner with a 1.97 ERA, 0.95 WHIP and 216 strikeouts in 187.2 innings. Seeing how that was his age-23 season, it was realistic to expect continued dominance for the foreseeable future.
However, he hasn't been the same in 2026 in part because of the drop in velocity.
Beazley noted Skenes averaged 98.8 mph on his fastball as a rookie and 98.1 in his second year. By comparison, his average this season is 96.8 mph.
Codify highlighted the recent fall off in his starts:
Fortunately for Skenes and the Pirates, he is still just 24 years old with plenty of time to bounce back. He also admitted he didn't train with a specific velocity in mind for the 2026 campaign, which was an unusual one that started earlier because of the World Baseball Classic.
There is no WBC in 2027, meaning he can go through a normal offseason and spring training ramp-up before taking the mound in his fourth season.
Perhaps that will help Skenes return to being one of the best pitchers in baseball like he was during his first two seasons.

Paul Skenes won the National League Cy Young Award last year, but has not had his best season this year.
Skenes was the National League Rookie of the Year in 2024, and looked like the best pitcher in baseball coming into the season. Through 55 career starts, he had a 1.96 ERA and 386 strikeouts. However, thgis year, he has a 3.91 ERA and his velocity is down. While every fan wonders what has happened to Skenes, he noted that the quick ramp-up for the World Baseball Classic may have played a role.
"There are a lot of other factors, so I don't want to put everything on that," Skenes told the Pittsburgh Post-Gazette's Colin Beazley. "But I feel like that was kind of the root of it a little bit."
"Usually, that time of year, you're kind of ramping up and it's a little bit slow. You can kind of get onto the slope and find your body," Skenes added. "One live (batting practice), you're topping at 97 (mph), and then the next you're 98, 99. And that wasn't the case this year. ... Looking back, I don't think that really helped."
Skenes made two starts in the World Baseball Classic, allowing one earned run in 8 1/3 innings of work. He was brilliant on the biggest stage, but perhaps the intensity of the event without a proper spring training build-up ended up hurting his numbers.
In 2024, his average fastball velocity was 98.8 mph. Last season it was 98.2 mph. This year, his four-seamer is sitting at 96.8 mph. It's a significant drop-off, but perhaps a full offseason with proper spring training will get him back on track next season.
"It definitely affected the year," Skenes said of the World Baseball Classic. "Unfortunately, I don't think I'm the only one."

Card collectors gather for trading card show at Independence Mall
WILMINGTON, NC (WWAY) — Trading card fanatics packed Independence Mall during the weekend to buy, trade, and sell trading cards.
Dozens of card collectors turned out over the weekend for a “TCG and Sports Card Show” at Independence Mall, where attendees could buy, trade and sell a wide variety of cards.
Some collectors arrived with briefcases, hoping to find the perfect addition to their collections. Cards ranged from Pokémon and baseball to hockey.
Friends Mitchell Smith and Britt Wilson shared some of their favorite cards.
“I’m a Duke fan, as you can tell. I like Cooper Flagg, so I have a Cooper Flagg autograph right now,” Smith said. “My favorite card in my collection is probably a Paul Skenes autograph,” said Wilson
Carolina Sports Promotions, which hosted the event, will return for the next card show at American Legion Post 10.

item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES — Philip Abner was going right back into the fire.
Abner had just made the wrong kind of history on Friday night, surrendering four homers in one inning. Max Muncy and Kyle Tucker went back-to-back to start the frame, then Mookie Betts and Will Smith did the same later in the inning. Following that disastrous outing, manager Tony Vitello said Abner would “be back out there at some point.”
That “some point” arrived less than 24 hours later. With the game on the line. In front of an announced attendance of 47,410. Considering the circumstances, Vitello’s decision was a true stunner. A night removed from the worst game of his career, Abner had to put out a fire at the game’s most critical point.
If this were Hollywood, maybe Abner would’ve enjoyed his redemption. But redemption never arrived. No feel-good story, no bounceback. Only an agonizing inning and the latest bizarre loss in a season full of them, a 10-4 defeat that had the makings of an upset win against back-to-back AL Cy Young Award winner Tarik Subal.
“Just needing to get one out. [He was] our only lefty in the bullpen, needing to get one out,” said manager Tony Vitello of the decision. “Other than our two guys that we want to finish with the game, you saw everybody we had available.”
When the Dodgers’ left-handed-hitting Josue De Paula stepped to the plate with two on and two outs, Abner was the team’s only available left-handed reliever to spell rookie Yunior Marte.
Reiver Sanmartín landed on the injured list before the game. Sam Hentges, who was activated from the injured list before the game, was unavailable, per Vitello. Matt Wilkinson was another option, but “Tugboat” is starting on Sunday. So, Abner.
That said, Vitello wasn’t required to seek out the left-on-left matchup. Especially since Abner had just become the first Giants pitcher to allow at least four homers in one inning since Alan Embree on May 20, 2001.
The hitter before De Paula, Kyle Tucker, was also left-handed, but Vitello left Marte face him. Vitello was likely saving Dylan Smith and Trent Harris for the later innings, but Kuhnel and Duncan Davitt, who he used in the sixth and seventh, were options.
Given how Friday unfolded, Vitello was asked if there was any consideration of steering clear of Abner.
“We avoided [Kyle] Tucker,” Vitello said. “But kind of what we got going on right now is finding out what you can and can’t do. And if I’m in his position, I’m dying to get back out there and see what I can do. I’ve had several guys come in the office, and we’ve had that conversation before. … Maybe we come up with a different plan, but otherwise, looking t get one out right there.” xr
Vitello added: “We talked about it last night and let him know that there’d be an opportunity around the corner. We knew Sanmartín was out. Sam wouldn’t be available based off his routine and his flight schedule and all that. So, we have talked about that.”
Abner’s first pitch foreshadowed what was to come, a bounced curveball that catcher Andrew Knizner couldn’t handle. He walked De Paula on five pitches, loading the bases for switch-hitter Tommy Edman.
Edman, who crushes lefties, pulled a single to left that scored Teoscar Hernández easily. Left fielder Turner Hill’s throw beat Kyle Tucker to the plate but was a tad off line and got away from Knizner. De Paula advanced to third, while Edman took second.
Following Edman’s two-run single, Miguel Rojas emerged from the Dodgers’ bench and rapped a single of his own. De Paula strolled home for Los Angeles’ third run of the inning, but a perfect throw by Hill nabbed Edman at the plate to mercifully end the inning and Abner’s night. Marte finished his night having allowed six runs over 4 2/3 innings.
“That’s just how baseball is,” Abner told this news organization when asked of the last two nights. “There’s too many games. You’re not going to be perfect all year. I definitely haven’t had the year that I’ve wanted. I’ve got one more week, and I’m going to make the most of it. Whatever happens, happens.”
Regarding Friday’s outing, in particular, Abner revealed that he had been tipping his pitches.
“Giving up four home runs sucks. It’s even worse when we were looking at video and found out I was tipping my pitches a little bit and telegraphing every single one of them,” Abner said. “Not even just fastball and offspeed. I worked on what to do to figure that out today. Walking my lefty isn’t exactly a good start, but I appreciate him letting me get back out there as soon as possible. It’s just one of those series. You’re going to have a bad series, and that’s just how it is.”
The bottom of the sixth featured a different flavor of agony as reliever Joel Kuhnel allowed three runs (one earned) due to a pair of misplays.
Shortstop Christian Koss committed an error when he dropped a throw on a force play from first baseman Brett Harris that would’ve been the second out. Two batters later, Harris could’ve been charged with an error after failing to corral a playable scoop from Koss that would’ve ended the inning. De Paula made Harris’ gaffe hurt, immediately driving in two more runs with a single.
The margin of defeat doesn’t reflect the Giants’ feistiness during the game’s first half. Thanks in large part to Victor Bericoto, San Francisco and Los Angeles entered the bottom of the fifth tied 4-4 as the Giants tagged Skubal for four runs.
Bericoto hit a no-doubt, two-run homer off Skubal on a middle-middle fastball in the third, emphatically throwing his bat before rounding the bases. The Giants scored a run in the fourth when Jonah Cox perfectly executed the squeeze play, then another in the fifth when Bericoto and Jung Hoo Lee hit back-to-back doubles, the latter driving in the former.
Then, that fateful bottom of the fifth.
For Skubal, it was the first time he allowed four runs in a game as a Dodger. This month alone, the Giants have scored nine combined runs off Skubal and Paul Skenes, the reigning Cy Young Award winners in both leagues. Despite those efforts, the Giants have lost both games.
Abner, 24, is one of many players fighting for a spot on next year’s roster. Realistically, with 16 players on the 60-day injured list and a wave of cuts coming, Abner could be looking at his final days in San Francisco. Regardless of what’s next, Abner is hoping for the best.
And to put the last two nights behind him.
“I’m definitely hoping they’ll keep me around,” Abner said. “It’s a long offseason. I’m going to do a lot to improve myself, so I’m hoping they’ll take a chance on me and keep it going from there.”

item.title: [MLB.com] These stars have turned their seasons around in the second half
item.dc:creator: Theo DeRosa
item.description: One well-timed hot streak from a star player can be all a team needs to go on a big run. item.content:encoded:
One well-timed hot streak from a star player can be all a team needs to go on a big run.
While many key contributors struggled in the first half of 2026, several have picked it up big time since the All-Star break, lifting their clubs to late-season success.
Here are 10 players -- five hitters and five pitchers -- who have turned things around in the second half.
All stats are through Saturday's games unless otherwise specified.
Hitters
Alex Bregman, Cubs
For as good as National League MVP Award favorite Pete Crow-Armstrong has been lately, it’s actually Bregman who entered Saturday leading all qualifying hitters with a 168 wRC+ in the second half. The third baseman has a .298/.376/.609 slash line since the All-Star break, with his 17 second-half homers tied for fourth most in MLB.
Batting just .241 with nine home runs and a .695 OPS prior to the break, Bregman hadn’t exactly been meeting expectations after signing a five-year, $175 million deal with the Cubs. Now, though, he is up to 5.1 FanGraphs WAR, his highest total since 2022 (5.4). He’s been a big reason the Cubs are currently on track to host an NL Wild Card Series at Wrigley Field, and he will be a key bat in the middle of Chicago’s lineup in the postseason.
Steven Kwan, Guardians
With this week’s series win over the White Sox, the Guardians have surged into first place in the AL Central, in large part thanks to their leadoff hitter’s resurgence. In addition to his strong defense in left field -- Kwan has won four straight AL Gold Gloves in left to begin his career -- Kwan has been on fire at the plate.
After a disappointing first-half slash line of .225/.332/.282, including a .188 batting average in May, Kwan ranks second among qualifiers with a .347 average and is tied with Yordan Alvarez for first with a .435 on-base percentage in the second half. He has been setting the table admirably for a Cleveland club not getting as much as usual from third baseman José Ramírez (94 wRC+) and could help the Guardians secure not only the division title but a key first-round bye.
Jackson Merrill, Padres
Merrill took a step back in 2025 after finishing second to the Pirates’ Paul Skenes in 2024 NL Rookie of the Year Award voting, and the Padres center fielder appeared headed for further regression based on early returns in 2026. Merrill’s OPS was below .600 in late May as San Diego scuffled offensively, and he took a .219/.278/.350 slash line into the break.
Since then, Merrill has been a major reason why the Padres have a 38-21 (.644) record in the second half, tied with the Brewers for the best in the NL. He’s hitting .312 with 16 home runs, 48 RBIs and a .944 OPS in 59 games in the second half while playing standout defense in center. Merrill’s ability to recapture his rookie form has given the Padres a fighting chance to host a Wild Card Series, and he’ll be a key middle-of-the-order bat for the club.
George Springer, Blue Jays
Springer improved his OPS by nearly 300 points from 2024 to 2025, slashing .309/.399/.560 and finishing seventh in AL MVP balloting as Toronto fell just short of a World Series title. But the veteran’s numbers fell off again early in 2026, especially after Springer returned from a stint on the injured list for a left big toe fracture. He hit just .218 with a .677 OPS before the All-Star break, a period of rest that seemed to help considerably.
Springer recorded multiple hits in five of his first nine second-half games, finishing July with an .878 OPS, before batting .321 with an .858 OPS in August. While he has slowed a bit in September, battling multiple injuries, he has clearly found his footing at the plate. It might not be enough to drag a Blue Jays team dealing with a host of pitching injuries and a down year from Vladimir Guerrero Jr. to the postseason, but Toronto -- three games out of an AL Wild Card spot -- still has a chance.
Fernando Tatis Jr., Padres
While Merrill’s turnaround has been integral to the Padres’ second-half surge, Tatis’ production out of the leadoff spot has perhaps been even more important. The three-time All-Star began the season by scorching the baseball into the ground, going 55 games before hitting his first home run of the year on May 30.
The second half brought on a true power surge for Tatis, who homered three times in his first four games after the All-Star break and is now up to 24 dingers on the season. Entering Saturday, his 167 wRC+ in the second half was second in MLB, behind only Bregman. Tatis has raised his season OPS to .819 and has given the Padres a dangerous option at leadoff down the stretch.
Pitchers
Brayan Bello, Red Sox
Bello has turned the page on a dismal start to the season. The right-hander, coming off a 3.35 ERA as a starter in 2025, had a 9.00 ERA in his first six starts of 2026 and was moved to a bulk-relief role. Still, Bello took a 6.06 ERA into the All-Star break as the Red Sox finally began to heat up, winning nine straight games to end the first half and extending the streak to a franchise record-tying 15.
Bello has continued to impress for Boston, earning the start on Saturday and baffling the Rays over eight innings of one-run ball with 11 strikeouts. In the midst of a statistically unprecedented season, he’s found something that works, which has been crucial for a Red Sox team that has surged into postseason position and appears headed for another clash with the Yankees in the AL Wild Card Series.
Robert Gasser, Brewers
Tommy John surgery in June 2024 cut short Gasser’s promising rookie season, but he returned to make two solid starts at the tail end of 2025. The left-hander couldn’t sustain that success early in 2026, taking a 5.24 ERA into the All-Star break after being tagged for seven runs in three innings in his final first-half start.
Since then, Gasser has a 3.00 ERA in 57 innings of work after holding the Orioles scoreless over seven excellent innings on Saturday in Baltimore. In his first four September outings, including two against the Cubs, he has allowed just four earned runs across 21 innings pitched. With Brandon Woodruff’s 2026 return questionable and Kyle Harrison struggling mightily, Gasser’s improvement has made him an important arm for a Milwaukee team fighting to secure the NL’s No. 1 seed.
Tyler Mahle, Braves
Mahle owned a 5.13 ERA through his first 18 starts of 2026 for the Giants, but the Braves saw something in the veteran right-hander. Atlanta acquired Mahle ahead of the Trade Deadline for righty reliever Anthony Molina in a move that has paid considerable dividends for the Braves’ battered rotation.
Mahle has allowed only seven earned runs in eight starts for Atlanta, completing six or more innings in all but one of those outings. His 1.28 ERA in that span is the third best among all pitchers (min. 40 innings), and he’s been an excellent complement to ace lefty Chris Sale atop the Braves rotation. With Spencer Strider, Spencer Schwellenbach, Bryce Elder, Reynaldo López and Hurston Waldrep all on the injured list, Mahle has not only covered important innings but has been remarkably effective.
Aaron Nola, Phillies
Nola had an ERA above 6 in an injury-marred 2025 season, and his 2026 looked to be more of the same. The usually dependable right-hander gave up 20 home runs in the first half alone, tied for the fifth most in MLB, and headed into the All-Star break with a 5.75 ERA.
Since then, Nola has returned to near-vintage form for the Phillies, who have also gotten strong second halves from lefty Jesús Luzardo (currently on the injured list with left shoulder inflammation) and rookie righty Andrew Painter. After Thursday’s excellent start against the Mets, Nola has a 2.78 ERA in the second half, striking out 67 in 71 1/3 innings despite giving up 14 more home runs in just 12 starts. If he can limit the long balls, he could be at least an adequate replacement for Luzardo if the southpaw cannot return for the start of the postseason.
Brandon Pfaadt, D-backs
Pfaadt hasn’t quite lived up to his billing as a former top prospect just yet, but he’s shown flashes, such as his success against the Dodgers and Phillies during the D-backs’ 2023 World Series run. The righty's recent results have been quite encouraging, too: Pfaadt has a 3.01 ERA in the second half, including a run of 27 2/3 scoreless innings across four starts from July 28-Aug. 14. 
Optioned to Triple-A Reno in June after a poor start to the year, Pfaadt now has the chance to help pitch the D-backs into the playoffs, which might be difficult in an NL Wild Card race featuring the Cubs, Phillies and Padres. Pfaadt is lined up to start during Arizona’s final series of the season, a pivotal three-game set in San Diego from Sept. 25-27, and his outing could determine the D-backs’ postseason fate.

item.content:encoded:
Garcia is thankful to be back in the starting lineup for the final days of the 2026 regular season. He has been limited to just 76 games, because of a partial tear of his left hamstring and just returned from the injured list on Tuesday after missing 21 games.
“I didn’t think I might play again this year, so I’m thankful,” Garcia said following Friday night’s 8-5 loss to the Pirates to open a three-game series at PNC Park. “I just wish there were more games left.”
Garcia had high hopes for 2026 after making his first All-Star Game appearance last season, then signing a five-year, $57.5 million contract extension that runs through 2030 and includes a club option for ‘31.
Alas, Garcia is slashing .262/.318/.378 with three home runs.
However, the 26-year-old provided a bright spot against Pittsburgh in what turned out to be a frustrating night for Kansas City. Garcia’s two-run double in the third inning helped the Royals build a 4-0 lead against reigning National League Cy Young winner Paul Skenes.
Still, they eventually lost for the 12th time in their last 17 games despite home runs by Vinnie Pasquantino and Michael Massey.
“We think the world of Mikey,” manager Matt Quatraro said of Garcia. “We committed a lot of years and a lot of money to him, because we think he’s a really good player who can help us win. Getting him back on the field is important for us, and it’s good for him, too.
“He probably thought his season was over, but he worked very hard through the rehab process to get back. And he got a big hit in a big spot.”
Just eight games remain for the Royals, so there isn’t a whole lot of season left to salvage for Garcia. Yet, he appreciates what few days remain and getting a big hit off a Cy Young winner.
“I like to face the best pitchers,” Garcia said with a smile. “It makes me fight that much harder. It felt really good to get a big hit there with a couple of guys on base. It’s been a tough year for me personally, but we have come back here, we want to finish the season healthy, and we want to help the team win some games. I want to go home for the winter with a good feeling.”
The usually unflappable Randy Dobnak admittedly was fighting some feelings when he took the mound in his hometown for just the second time in his career. The right-hander grew up in suburban South Park, Pa.
Dobnak’s previous appearance at PNC Park came with the Twins in 2020. However, fans weren’t permitted to attend games during that pandemic-shortened season. Dobnak estimated he had at least 200 family members and friends in the stands and had attended approximately 300 games in this ballpark.
“This was really kind of special,” Dobnak said. “After I threw my last warm-up pitch, I stood there on the mound and took it all in. Growing up, this was the place I always wanted to be. I caught myself almost getting a little bit emotional out there.”
Dobnak paused and chuckled.
“That quickly changed when I threw my first pitch and [Konnor] Griffin singled right back up the middle,” he said.
Unfortunately for Dobnak and his throng of supporters, that signaled what was to come. He lasted just 3 2/3 innings and gave up four runs on seven hits and two walks, while striking out one.
Dobnak left with a 5-3 lead, but the Pirates rallied against the Royals’ bullpen. Spencer Horwitz’s two-run single off Nate Pearson in a three-run seventh inning broke a 5-5 tie.
“I think the biggest thing was first-pitch strikes with Randy,” Quatraro said. “It was an interesting game for him. There were four hits down the third-base line from a left-handed hitter and a couple of infield hits. He had a lot of traffic to deal with.”

item.content:encoded:
Livvy Dunne Dismisses Fantasy Baseball Manager's Paul Skenes Request With 'South Park' Meme
Don't bother Livvy Dunne with complaints about how Paul Skenes is impacting your fantasy baseball team.
After Dunne posted a TikTok video showing her doing gymnastics exercises, a fan in the comments decided to write a snarky message asking her to tell Skenes to "do good for my fantasy" team.
Rather than let the message slide, Dunne replied with a South Park meme featuring Stan saying "Dude, we don't care."

It's hard to argue Skenes hasn't helped fantasy teams this season. He's obviously not pitching as well as he did in 2024 or 2025, but his 3.78 ERA and 185 strikeouts in 162 innings is far from terrible.
Sure, Skenes only ranks 32nd among all starting pitchers in total fantasy points entering Friday. He is right around Tarik Skubal, Jacob deGrom and Nolan McLean.
This has been a strange season for many pitchers. Not many people would have guessed in April that Jesús Luzardo, Drew Rasmussen and Parker Messick were going to be top-eight fantasy starters.
